p:NLD: The Netherlands uses the euro, whose rates the European Central Bank sets for the 21 countries on it, and De Nederlandsche Bank is the Dutch central bank inside that system; it scores 23 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In June 2010 the Scheltema committee, set up by finance minister Wouter Bos, found that the bank had fallen seriously short in supervising DSB bank, missing flaws when licensing DSB in 2005 and being too patient afterwards, though it thought a different approach probably would not have prevented DSB's collapse. Parliament pressed the bank hard after that report: members called for a major overhaul of how it operates, the Christian Democrats said it had seriously fallen short as a regulator and that president Nout Wellink should explain publicly how he would restore its credibility, the GroenLinks member Jolande Sap said it would be very difficult to keep him on, and Roland van Vliet of the Freedom Party asked finance minister Jan Kees de Jager to sack him with a year of his term still to run. On 1 July 2010 the lower house voted on a motion of no confidence in Wellink and he survived it. He accepted the report's conclusions, which several members said was enough for them, and left at the end of his term in 2011. Two further findings sit at the European Central Bank: the European Ombudsman, the European Union's complaints office, found maladministration over president Mario Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a forum of central bankers and private financiers, and in January 2018 recommended he suspend it, which the bank declined and he did not; and a board member's 18 May 2015 remarks in London that the bank would front-load asset purchases were published only the next morning, which the bank put down to an internal procedure error. Wim Duisenberg joined the Dutch bank in 1981 and became chairman in 1982, after three years at the International Monetary Fund and a seat on Rabobank's board. Most of its gold is stored for it rather than managed: 32 per cent at the Bank of England, 18.5 per cent at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and 18.5 per cent at the Royal Canadian Mint in Ottawa. EY Accountants B.V. audits the accounts for 2026 to 2032.
p:SVN: Slovenia uses the euro, so the Bank of Slovenia does not set interest rates itself; the European Central Bank sets them for the 21 countries using the euro. Both are among the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. The main local matter is the 2013 bank bailout, in which a 960 million euro bail-in, meaning losses forced on investors, hit about 100,000 junior bondholders and shareholders. Police have filed a second criminal complaint alleging abuse of office over it, after a 2016 attempt hit a dead end over procedural errors; the specialised prosecutor has asked the court to investigate, so nothing is proven. That inquiry included a search of the bank's premises on 6 July 2016, over which the European Central Bank's President wrote to Slovenia's prosecutor general and to the European Commission about information seized. The police took all communications from the governor's email account, every electronic document in his workspace and on his laptop dated between 2012 and 2014 whatever its content, part of the paper files in his office from those years and documents from the bank's central IT server, and went ahead without involving the European Central Bank after the bank objected. On 17 December 2020 the Court of Justice of the European Union held, in Commission v Slovenia, that the material seized must have included documents forming part of the European Central Bank's archives and that Slovenia had infringed their inviolability; it also held that Slovenia then failed to cooperate, by not letting the bank identify which seized documents related to central bank tasks and by not returning even those the authorities themselves regarded as irrelevant to the investigation. Two findings concern the European Central Bank itself: on 18 May 2015 Benoit Coeure told a private London event it would front-load asset purchases before the speech was published; and in January 2018 the European Ombudsman found maladministration and asked Mario Draghi to suspend his membership of the Group of Thirty, a private forum of central bankers and financiers, which the bank declined. Six career moves are recorded between that board and private finance, among them Otmar Issing advising Goldman Sachs and Lorenzo Bini Smaghi leaving to chair Societe Generale, with no ethics finding on them. Slovenia scores 22 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:SWE: Sveriges Riksbank is Sweden's central bank and issues the krona. It scores 15 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, less exposed than 99 per cent of the 194 places with a figure. The Riksdag adopted a new Sveriges Riksbank Act on 23 November 2022, in force from 1 January 2023. The inquiry that preceded it proposed limits on what the Riksbank may do in monetary policy, which its Executive Board objected to in its consultation response and some of which were dropped from the final Act. What stayed includes a requirement of exceptional grounds before the bank may buy or sell financial instruments other than Swedish government securities for monetary policy purposes, on the reasoning that such trading carries much greater financial risk for the bank and for state finances; limits on its equity and a cap on borrowing for the foreign exchange reserve; and an obligation to ask the Riksdag to restore its equity when that falls below the floor, which it had to do after the bond purchases it made earlier lost money as rates rose. The Riksdag also now approves the specification of the inflation target. The bank's own account is two-sided: it says the Act leaves it a strong and clear mandate and carries the ban on taking instructions over unchanged, while governor Erik Thedeen said after a year of it that the governance is too strong on strengthening the foreign exchange reserve and on buying securities for financial stability purposes. Two linked cases run from 2020 to 2021. On 18 June 2021 the Riksbank said a routine check of staff securities dealings had found a few employees making transactions that did not fit its ethics rules, including share trades close to monetary policy decisions and trades in companies whose corporate bonds it was buying; it called this inappropriate, held talks with those involved and began revising the rules. After media reports that Stefan Ingves and Skingsley had conflicts of interest from shares they held while deciding on corporate bond purchases, the bank's General Council reviewed the matter and on 17 December 2021 concluded the link was too weak to amount to a conflict of interest, finding no shortcoming in their conduct. Ingves was appointed governor in October 2005, having headed a department at the International Monetary Fund since 1999; that move is not an accusation. Its 125.7 tonnes of gold sit partly at the Riksbank and partly abroad, 61.4 tonnes at the Bank of England, 33.2 at the Bank of Canada, 13.2 at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and 2.8 at the Swiss National Bank, which is storage of the gold and not management of its money. Crane AB printed the notes at Tumba until the Riksbank gave notice to end the contract on 19 June 2018 because Crane was moving printing to Malta; De La Rue replaced it under an agreement announced on 19 September 2018.
